planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; this species tolerates chalky ground poorly suited to common lilac.

directions: Unlike nearly every other lilac grown in gardens, this western Chinese species has compound, fern-like pinnate leaves with up to eleven small leaflets rather than the familiar simple heart-shaped lilac leaf, giving the shrub an airy, fine-textured look even out of bloom. In mid-spring it opens loose clusters of small white flowers lightly flushed with mauve, followed by attractive peeling bark as the stems mature. It flowers earlier and more modestly than Syringa vulgaris, so site it where its distinctive foliage can be appreciated through the rest of the season. Give it chalky or neutral, well-drained soil and full sun, and avoid the heavy, wet clay that stresses most lilac species.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Bean's Trees and Shrubs)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in fall or spring in full sun and moist, well-drained soil; allow room for wide-arching branches.

directions: Nodding lilac takes its name from its long, slender flower panicles, which droop and arch downward at the branch tips rather than standing upright like most lilac species, giving the whole shrub a graceful, weeping appearance in late spring. The purplish-pink buds open to pink flowers with pale interiors, held against broad, mid-green oval leaves. Native to central China, it is among the cold-hardiest lilac species and tolerates harsh continental winters that damage less hardy garden lilacs. Give it full sun and well-drained soil with room to spread, since mature plants develop a wide, arching habit.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun with some shelter from harsh winter wind; root-hardy even where top growth is damaged by cold.

directions: This Himalayan species stands out among butterfly bushes for its broad, wavy-edged gray-green leaves densely coated in white felted hairs, giving the whole plant a soft, silvery cast even before it blooms. Short terminal spikes of fragrant lilac flowers with orange throats appear in late summer and draw butterflies and hummingbirds in large numbers. It is less reliably cold-hardy than Buddleja davidii and may die back to the ground in harsh winters, but it regrows readily from the base since it is root hardy well below where top growth survives. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, and avoid overly rich, wet soil that softens its naturally drought-tolerant growth.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; fast growing and tolerant of heat and drought once established.

directions: Sagewood is a large, fast-growing South African shrub named for its wrinkled, gray-green leaves whose sage-like undersides are coated in dense white felt. From midwinter into spring it carries long, arching sprays of small, honey-scented flowers in shades of cream to pale lilac that draw bees and other pollinators in great numbers. Its loose, multi-stemmed, somewhat untidy habit makes it best suited to larger gardens or informal screens rather than tight borders. It is notably drought and heat tolerant once established and takes hard pruning well, making it useful as a quick-growing windbreak or background shrub in mild-winter climates.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Bean's Trees and Shrubs)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in a sheltered, sunny site with well-drained soil; protect from cold, drying winds and winter wet in marginal zones.

directions: Winter buddleja breaks from the usual butterfly bush pattern by flowering in late winter and early spring rather than summer, opening slender terminal spikes of small, intensely sweet-scented white flowers while most other shrubs are still dormant. Its long, widely spaced leaves are dark green above and felted gray beneath, giving the evergreen foliage a two-toned look. Native across a broad swath of Asia from the Himalayas to Indonesia, it is only reliably hardy in warm, frost-free gardens and needs a sheltered position where cold, drying wind and waterlogged winter soil are not a problem. Where marginal, grow it against a warm wall or in a container that can be moved under cover for winter.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Bean's Trees and Shrubs)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; forms a dense, spiny, impenetrable thicket useful for barrier plantings.

directions: This West Chinese species carries narrow, lance-shaped evergreen leaves edged with fine spiny teeth along stiff, thorny branches, giving it one of the most formidable barrier habits of any evergreen barberry. Clusters of small yellow flowers appear in early summer, followed by waxy, blue-black oblong berries that persist into winter and attract birds. Its dense, wiry growth and sharp spines make it an effective security hedge or deterrent planting that needs little pruning to stay thick. Grow it in any well-drained soil in sun to light shade; it tolerates dry spells well once established but resents waterlogged ground.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Bean's Trees and Shrubs)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to light shade and well-drained soil; very cold-hardy and reliable in short-season northern climates.

directions: Native to the Amur region of eastern Siberia, northeast China, and Korea, this mock orange is prized for extreme cold tolerance and a dense, upright, fast-growing habit that quickly fills in as a hedge or background shrub. It opens its pure white, four-petaled flowers earlier in the season than most other Philadelphus species, though the blooms carry little to no fragrance, trading the classic mock-orange scent for reliability in harsh winters. Full sun brings the heaviest flowering, but light shade is tolerated without much loss of vigor. Renew older stems by thinning out a portion of the oldest wood right after flowering to keep the shrub full and floriferous.
